---
title: "Psychology, Behaviour, and Decision-Making（心理、行为与决策）"
---

## Perception and Human Interpretation（感知与人的解释）

Perception（感知）transforms raw sensory input（原始感觉输入）into organised, meaningful experience. Vision, hearing, touch, taste, and smell receive physical energy from the environment — patterns of light waves（光波）, air vibrations（空气振动）, chemical compounds（化合物）, pressure on the skin（皮肤压力）, and temperature variations（温度变化）. The brain actively selects, organises, and interprets this sensory data, constructing a coherent representation（连贯表征）of the world that guides action and decision-making. Perception operates as an active construction（主动建构）rather than a passive recording of reality — the brain uses prior knowledge（先前知识）, expectations（期望）, and context（语境）to fill in gaps, resolve ambiguity（解决歧义）, and generate the experience that reaches conscious awareness（意识觉知）.

Perception is fundamentally selective（选择性的）. At any moment, the senses receive far more information than the brain can process fully. The visual system（视觉系统）alone receives millions of bits of information per second, but conscious awareness can handle only a tiny fraction. The brain must choose what to attend to and what to filter out（过滤）. This selection is influenced by expectations, prior knowledge, current goals, and emotional state（情绪状态）. In a crowded room, a familiar face captures attention immediately because it carries personal significance, while most other faces are processed only at a superficial level and never reach awareness. This selective attention（选择性注意）is essential for functioning in an environment that constantly presents more information than any cognitive system could handle simultaneously.

Bottom-up processing（自下而上加工）builds perception from the sensory data itself — the raw features（原始特征）of lines, edges, colours, movements, and sounds that arrive at the sensory receptors（感受器）. Top-down processing（自上而下加工）builds perception from prior knowledge, expectations, and context — the brain's predictions about what should be present given the situation. Most perception involves both processes operating simultaneously. When reading, bottom-up processing recognises individual letters and letter combinations, while top-down processing uses knowledge of language structure（语言结构）and context to predict upcoming words and resolve ambiguous text. Skilled readers rely heavily on top-down processing, which allows rapid, efficient reading — they do not decode every letter individually but use context to predict and confirm word identity（词汇识别）.

Context（语境 / 情境）influences perception at every level of processing. The same sensory input can be interpreted differently depending on the surrounding situation. A person running toward another in a park during the day is perceived as a jogger（慢跑者）; the same action in a dark alley at night is perceived as a potential threat（潜在威胁）. The brain uses context to resolve ambiguity and generate the most probable interpretation（最可能的解释）of incoming sensory data. This context-dependence（语境依赖性）is usually adaptive — it allows the brain to make quick, accurate interpretations based on experience and situational cues（情境线索）. It can also produce errors when the context is misleading or when prior expectations override actual sensory evidence.

Perceptual organisation（知觉组织）follows principles identified by Gestalt psychologists（格式塔心理学家）that describe how the brain groups individual sensory elements into coherent wholes. The brain tends to group elements that are spatially close (proximity / 接近性), similar in appearance (similarity / 相似性), or form continuous patterns (continuity / 连续性). It tends to perceive complete shapes even when parts are missing (closure / 闭合性), and it separates objects from their backgrounds (figure-ground segregation / 图形-背景分离). These principles reflect the brain's tendency to impose structure on sensory input — organising it into meaningful objects and scenes rather than processing it as a collection of unrelated features. This organisation occurs automatically and pre-consciously（前意识地）, before the perceiver is aware of the individual elements.

Perceptual illusions（感知错觉）demonstrate that perception is constructed rather than directly recorded from the environment. In visual illusions（视觉错觉）, the brain's assumptions about how the physical world works produce perceptions that systematically depart from physical reality. The Müller-Lyer illusion — where two lines of equal length appear different because of the direction of arrowheads at their ends — shows that the brain's assumptions about depth（深度）and perspective（透视）can override actual retinal measurements. The Ponzo illusion — where converging lines create an impression of depth, making equal objects appear different in size — demonstrates how the brain uses perspective cues（透视线索）to scale perceived size. These illusions are systematic errors of the normal perceptual system — they reveal the constructive processes that usually produce accurate perception, becoming visible only when those processes are applied to specially designed stimuli（刺激）.

Depth perception（深度知觉）illustrates how the brain constructs a three-dimensional experience（三维体验）from two-dimensional retinal images（二维视网膜图像）. The brain combines multiple cues: binocular disparity（双眼视差）— the slight difference between the images projected onto the two retinas, which provides precise depth information for nearby objects; motion parallax（运动视差）— the fact that nearby objects appear to move faster than distant ones when the observer moves, providing depth information during locomotion（运动）; and pictorial cues（图画线索）such as relative size（相对大小）, texture gradient（纹理梯度）, linear perspective（线性透视）, occlusion（遮挡）, and shading（阴影）. These cues are combined automatically and unconsciously to produce the seamless experience of a three-dimensional world.

Perception therefore transforms raw sensory data into organised, meaningful experience through selection, context, prior knowledge, and automatic interpretive processes. The vocabulary of perception — bottom-up processing, top-down processing, selective attention, perceptual organisation, Gestalt principles, perceptual illusion, depth perception, binocular disparity — names the mechanisms through which the brain constructs a coherent experience of the world from fragmentary sensory input. Psychological texts use this vocabulary to trace the pathways from sensory input through perceptual organisation to the conscious experience that guides human action and decision-making.

## Attention and Cognitive Limits（注意力与认知限制）

Attention（注意力）is the cognitive process（认知过程）of selectively focusing mental resources on specific information while suppressing（抑制）other information. Attention is fundamentally limited — the brain cannot attend to everything simultaneously. This limitation is a necessary feature of a system with finite processing capacity（有限加工容量）. If the brain processed all incoming information equally, it would be overwhelmed by the constant stream of sensory input, unable to prioritise what matters, and incapable of coherent action. Attention solves this problem by allocating processing resources to the most relevant information at each moment.

Selective attention（选择性注意）allows focus on one source of information while filtering out competing sources. In a noisy room, one conversation can be followed while background noise is suppressed — the cocktail party effect（鸡尾酒会效应）. This ability is essential for functioning in complex environments where multiple stimuli（刺激）compete for limited cognitive resources. Selective attention operates through both early and late filtering mechanisms. Early selection（早期选择）filters irrelevant information before it is fully processed — preventing it from consuming processing resources. Late selection（晚期选择）processes all information to some degree but allows only attended information to reach conscious awareness and guide behaviour. Evidence supports a combination: some filtering occurs early in the processing stream, but even unattended information receives partial processing — as demonstrated when a person hears their own name in an unattended conversation, a phenomenon showing that semantic processing（语义加工）can occur outside focal attention（焦点注意）.

Divided attention（分配性注意）is the attempt to attend to multiple tasks simultaneously. People often believe they can multitask（多任务处理）effectively, but research consistently shows that attention is severely limited when performing multiple attention-demanding tasks. When people attempt two cognitively demanding tasks at once, performance on both tasks deteriorates（下降）. Talking on a phone while driving increases accident risk（事故风险）because the brain cannot fully allocate attention to both tasks — the driving task receives less processing, reaction times（反应时间）slow, and the driver may fail to notice hazards（危险）. The secondary task also suffers, as the driver misses parts of the conversation or provides less coherent responses. The impairment（损害）from phone use while driving is comparable in magnitude to the impairment from alcohol intoxication（酒精中毒）at the legal limit.

Task switching（任务切换）is fundamentally different from simultaneous multitasking. When people appear to multitask, they are typically switching rapidly between tasks rather than processing them in parallel. Each switch carries a cognitive cost（认知代价）— time and mental energy are consumed in disengaging from（脱离）one task, reconfiguring（重新配置）the cognitive system for the new task, and re-engaging with（重新投入）its specific requirements. Frequent task switching reduces overall efficiency（整体效率）and increases errors（错误率）. This is why working in an environment with constant interruptions（持续干扰）— phone calls, emails, messages, notifications — reduces productivity（生产率）even though each individual interruption is brief. The cumulative cost of repeated switching can consume a substantial portion of the working day.

Cognitive load（认知负荷）refers to the total mental effort being used in working memory（工作记忆）at any given time. When cognitive load exceeds available capacity, learning and performance suffer. Cognitive load theory（认知负荷理论）distinguishes three types. Intrinsic cognitive load（内在认知负荷）is the inherent difficulty of the material itself — learning quantum mechanics（量子力学）has higher intrinsic load than learning basic arithmetic（基本算术）because the concepts are more complex and abstract. Extraneous cognitive load（外在认知负荷）is caused by how the material is presented — a poorly designed diagram（设计不良的图表）, confusing instructions（令人困惑的说明）, or split attention（注意力分散）between multiple information sources adds unnecessary load that does not contribute to learning. Germane cognitive load（相关认知负荷）is the productive mental effort devoted to building mental models（心智模型）, integrating new information with existing knowledge, and constructing schemas（图式建构）.

Effective instruction manages cognitive load by reducing extraneous load, optimising intrinsic load through appropriate sequencing（合理排序）and scaffolding（支架式教学）, and maximising germane load through activities that promote deep processing. Presenting information in manageable chunks（可管理的组块）, using clear and well-designed visual materials（清晰的视觉材料）, providing worked examples（示范例题）, integrating text and diagrams spatially（空间整合文字与图表）rather than separating them, and building on prior knowledge all reduce unnecessary cognitive load. A text that introduces too many new concepts simultaneously can overwhelm cognitive capacity, making comprehension impossible regardless of the reader's general ability or motivation.

Attention therefore functions as the mechanism that allocates limited mental resources to the most important information and tasks. The vocabulary of attention — selective attention, divided attention, cocktail party effect, task switching, cognitive load, intrinsic load, extraneous load, germane load — names the processes through which the brain manages its finite processing capacity and the conditions that determine whether cognitive resources are used efficiently or wasted. Psychological texts use this vocabulary to trace the pathways from attention allocation through cognitive load management to the learning and performance outcomes that determine whether people can process information effectively in complex environments.

## Memory, Recall, and Distortion（记忆、回忆与扭曲）

Memory（记忆）is the cognitive system that encodes（编码）, stores（存储）, and retrieves（提取）information across time. Memory is not a single unitary system but consists of multiple interacting subsystems（子系统）, each with different characteristics, capacities, and functions. The three main stages of memory processing are encoding — transforming experience into a neural representation; storage — maintaining that representation over time; and retrieval — accessing the stored representation when needed. A failure at any stage can result in forgetting（遗忘）: information may never have been encoded effectively, may have decayed（衰退）or been overwritten（覆盖）during storage, or may be stored but inaccessible because appropriate retrieval cues（提取线索）are absent.

The multi-store model（多存储模型）distinguishes three memory systems with different durations and capacities. Sensory memory（感觉记忆）holds sensory information for a very brief period — less than a second for visual information (iconic memory / 图像记忆) and a few seconds for auditory information (echoic memory / 回声记忆). It acts as a buffer（缓冲器）, holding information long enough for the brain to decide whether it is important enough to attend to and transfer to the next stage. Short-term memory（短时记忆）holds a small amount of information — approximately seven items (plus or minus two), a finding known as Miller's Law（米勒定律）— for about twenty to thirty seconds without rehearsal（复述）. Working memory（工作记忆）is the active component of short-term memory that processes and manipulates information — it is the mental workspace（心理工作空间）where thinking happens, where information is combined, compared, transformed, and used to guide behaviour. Working memory capacity varies between individuals and is a strong predictor（预测因子）of intelligence（智力）and reasoning ability（推理能力）.

Long-term memory（长时记忆）stores information for extended periods — from minutes to an entire lifetime. Its capacity is effectively unlimited（实际上无限的）. Long-term memory is divided into explicit memory（外显记忆）— memories that can be consciously recalled and verbally described — and implicit memory（内隐记忆）— memories that influence behaviour without conscious awareness. Explicit memory includes episodic memory（情景记忆）— memories of specific personal events and experiences, including when and where they occurred — and semantic memory（语义记忆）— general knowledge about the world, concepts, facts, and meanings that are not tied to a specific personal experience. Implicit memory includes procedural memory（程序记忆）— skills and habits such as riding a bicycle or typing — and priming effects（启动效应）— where prior exposure to a stimulus influences responses to subsequent stimuli without conscious awareness.

Forgetting follows a predictable pattern described by the forgetting curve（遗忘曲线）, first documented by Hermann Ebbinghaus. Information is forgotten rapidly at first — approximately fifty percent within an hour — then more slowly over time. Without review or rehearsal, most new information is largely forgotten within days. The rate of forgetting depends on the depth of initial encoding（初始编码深度）: information that is processed deeply — connected to existing knowledge, elaborated（精细加工）, given personal meaning, or practised through retrieval — is forgotten more slowly than information processed superficially through simple repetition（简单重复）or passive exposure（被动接触）.

Spaced repetition（间隔重复）— reviewing material at increasing intervals — is an effective learning strategy because it exploits the forgetting curve. Each review session（复习环节）strengthens the memory trace（记忆痕迹）and extends how long the information lasts before the next review is needed. The optimal review schedule（最佳复习计划）spaces reviews just before the information would be forgotten, maximising the strengthening effect of each retrieval attempt. This spacing effect（间隔效应）is one of the most robust findings in memory research and applies across ages, materials, and educational contexts.

Memory is reconstructive（重建性的）rather than a faithful recording（忠实记录）of past events. When an event is recalled, it is not retrieved as a complete, unaltered record; it is reconstructed from fragments（碎片）, with gaps filled in by what seems plausible given the person's general knowledge, expectations, and current context. This reconstructive nature makes memory vulnerable to distortion（扭曲）. The misinformation effect（误导信息效应）occurs when exposure to misleading information after an event alters the memory of that event. Leading questions（引导性问题）— "How fast were the cars going when they smashed into each other?" versus "How fast were the cars going when they hit each other?" — change what witnesses remember, with "smashed" producing higher speed estimates and more false memories（虚假记忆）of broken glass that did not exist. Source monitoring errors（来源监控错误）occur when the brain correctly remembers information but incorrectly remembers where it came from — a person may remember a fact but forget whether they learned it from a reliable textbook or an unreliable website, potentially treating unverified information as authoritative（权威性的）.

Active recall（主动回忆）— testing oneself on material rather than simply rereading it — is one of the most effective methods for strengthening memory. The act of retrieving information from memory strengthens the memory trace and makes it more accessible in future retrieval attempts. This testing effect（测试效应）means that taking practice tests produces better long-term retention than additional study time spent rereading. Organising information into meaningful patterns（有意义的模式）, creating connections between new and existing knowledge, and using elaboration strategies all improve memory by creating multiple retrieval pathways（多条提取路径）that increase the probability of successful recall.

Memory therefore functions as the system that encodes, stores, and retrieves information across time, enabling learning, identity, and decision-making. The vocabulary of memory — sensory memory, short-term memory, working memory, long-term memory, explicit memory, implicit memory, episodic memory, semantic memory, forgetting curve, spaced repetition, misinformation effect, source monitoring error, testing effect — names the processes through which information is encoded, stored, and retrieved, and how these processes can be improved or disrupted. Psychological texts use this vocabulary to trace the pathways from encoding through storage to the retrieval outcomes that determine whether people can access the knowledge and experiences they need to function effectively in daily life.

## Emotion and Judgement（情绪与判断）

Emotion（情绪）is a complex psychological state involving subjective experience（主观体验）, physiological response（生理反应）, and behavioural expression（行为表达）. Emotions influence how people think, what they attend to, how they interpret events, and how they make decisions. Emotion and cognition（认知）are deeply interconnected — they are not separate systems operating independently but interacting processes that shape each other continuously.

The somatic marker hypothesis（躯体标记假说）, proposed by neuroscientist Antonio Damasio, suggests that emotions guide decision-making by providing bodily signals（身体信号）that mark options as good or bad based on prior experience. Patients with damage to brain regions involved in emotion processing（情绪加工脑区）— particularly the ventromedial prefrontal cortex（腹内侧前额叶皮层）— often make poor decisions despite intact logical reasoning abilities（完整的逻辑推理能力）. They can analyse options rationally but cannot assign emotional value（情感价值）to different choices, making it difficult to choose among options with similar logical merits. This finding demonstrates that effective decision-making requires emotional input — pure reason without emotion produces indecision（优柔寡断）and poor choices rather than optimal outcomes.

Emotions affect judgement systematically through mood-congruent processing（情绪一致性加工）. When people are in a positive mood（积极情绪）, they tend to make more optimistic judgements, perceive lower risk, and process information more broadly using heuristic processing（启发式加工）— quick, intuitive thinking that relies on mental shortcuts. When they are in a negative mood（消极情绪）, they tend to make more pessimistic judgements, perceive higher risk, and process information more carefully using systematic processing（系统化加工）— detailed, analytical thinking that examines evidence thoroughly. A person who is anxious（焦虑的）about a medical test may judge the probability of a negative result as higher than objective evidence warrants, because anxiety activates threat-related schemas（威胁相关图式）that bias probability estimates（概率估计）.

The affect heuristic（情感启发式）describes how people make judgements based on their immediate emotional response（即时情绪反应）rather than on deliberate analysis. If something feels good, people tend to judge it as beneficial and low-risk. If something feels bad, they judge it as harmful and high-risk. This heuristic is often efficient — emotional responses evolved to provide rapid assessments（快速评估）of whether situations, objects, or people are safe or dangerous, and they often capture important information that deliberate analysis might miss. The affect heuristic can also produce systematic errors when emotional responses are triggered by irrelevant factors — people may judge a technology as risky because it evokes fear（恐惧）(nuclear power / 核能) while judging a familiar activity as safe despite high statistical risk (driving / 驾驶).

Emotional arousal（情绪唤醒）— the intensity of emotional activation — affects memory through emotional memory enhancement（情绪记忆增强）. Events that trigger strong emotions are often remembered more vividly（更生动地）and for longer than neutral events, because emotional arousal activates the amygdala（杏仁核）, which modulates（调节）memory consolidation（记忆巩固）in the hippocampus（海马体）. This mechanism signals to the brain that emotionally significant information is important and worth retaining. However, emotional arousal also narrows attention（窄化注意力）, causing people to focus on central emotional details while missing peripheral information（外围信息）— a phenomenon called weapon focus（武器聚焦）in eyewitness testimony（目击证词）, where witnesses to a crime remember the weapon vividly but cannot accurately describe the perpetrator's face or clothing.

Emotion regulation（情绪调节）is the ability to manage and respond to emotional experiences in ways that are appropriate to the situation and consistent with personal goals. Different regulation strategies（调节策略）have different effectiveness and consequences. Cognitive reappraisal（认知重评）— changing how one interprets a situation to alter its emotional impact — is generally effective and associated with better psychological outcomes（心理结果）. A student who reframes exam anxiety（考试焦虑）as excitement about demonstrating their knowledge changes the emotional experience without suppressing it. Expressive suppression（表达抑制）— hiding outward emotional expressions — is less effective because it does not reduce the internal emotional experience and consumes cognitive resources that could be used for other tasks. Emotion regulation can be learned and improved through practice, therapy（治疗）, and mindfulness training（正念训练）.

Emotion therefore functions as a system that guides decision-making, shapes judgement, and modulates memory through physiological and cognitive mechanisms. The vocabulary of emotion — somatic marker hypothesis, heuristic processing, systematic processing, affect heuristic, emotional arousal, emotional memory enhancement, emotion regulation, cognitive reappraisal — names the processes through which emotional states influence thinking, memory, and decision-making. Psychological texts use this vocabulary to trace the pathways from emotional triggers through cognitive and physiological responses to the behavioural outcomes that determine whether emotions help or hinder effective decision-making.

## Habit Formation and Behavioural Patterns（习惯形成与行为模式）

Habits（习惯）are automatic behaviours（自动行为）triggered by specific environmental cues（环境线索）. Once a habit is formed, it can be performed with minimal conscious thought or effort, freeing cognitive resources for other tasks. Habits are stored in neural systems（神经系统）— particularly the basal ganglia（基底神经节）— that operate independently of conscious goals and intentions（意图）. This independence explains why habits can persist even when the person consciously wants to change them — the habit system responds to cues automatically, bypassing the deliberative system（审慎系统）that evaluates goals and consequences.

Habit formation（习惯形成）follows a three-component loop（三组件循环）: cue（提示）, routine（惯例 / 行为）, and reward（奖励）. The cue is a trigger that signals the brain to initiate the habitual behaviour. Cues can be a time of day, a location, an emotional state（情绪状态）, a preceding action, or the presence of specific people. The routine is the behaviour itself — the action performed automatically in response to the cue. The reward is the positive outcome or feeling that reinforces the habit, teaching the brain that the routine is worth remembering and repeating. Over time, the brain learns to associate the cue with the reward through the routine, and neural connections（神经连接）between the cue and the routine strengthen with each repetition. The anticipation of the reward（奖励预期）creates a craving（渴望）that drives the behaviour even before the reward is received — the cue alone triggers the urge to perform the routine.

The habit of checking a phone when a notification sounds follows this loop precisely. The notification sound is the cue. Picking up and looking at the phone is the routine. The new information, social connection, or entertainment is the reward. Each repetition strengthens the neural association between the sound and the checking behaviour. Over time, the sound triggers an almost irresistible urge（不可抵抗的冲动）to check, even when the person knows the notification is probably unimportant. The same mechanism operates in habits ranging from nail-biting（咬指甲）to exercise routines（运动习惯）to dietary patterns（饮食模式）— each involves a cue that triggers a routine in anticipation of a reward.

Changing a habit requires understanding and working with the habit loop rather than relying on willpower（意志力）alone. The most effective strategy is to change the routine while preserving the same cue and the same reward. To stop checking social media（社交媒体）when bored, the routine could be replaced with taking a short walk or doing a breathing exercise（呼吸练习）. The cue (boredom / 无聊) and the reward (relief from boredom / 无聊的缓解) remain the same, but the new routine provides a healthier way to achieve the same psychological outcome. Attempting to simply suppress（压制）the habit without replacing the routine often fails because the cue continues to trigger craving and the unmet craving intensifies over time.

Implementation intentions（实施意向）are specific plans that link a situational cue to a desired behaviour: "When X happens, I will do Y." Research shows that forming implementation intentions dramatically increases the likelihood of following through on goals（目标执行）. The vague intention "I will exercise more" provides no specific cue to trigger action and is easily displaced by competing demands. The implementation intention "When I finish work at 5 PM, I will change into my running shoes and go for a 30-minute run" creates a strong cue-behaviour association（线索-行为关联）that can become automatic over time. Implementation intentions work because they delegate the initiation of behaviour to an external cue, reducing the need for conscious decision-making（有意识的决策）at the moment of action.

Habit formation therefore represents the mechanism through which repeated behaviours become automatic and how they can be changed by understanding and modifying the components of the habit loop. The vocabulary of habit — cue, routine, reward, craving, implementation intention, automaticity, habit loop — names the processes through which behaviours become automatic and the intervention strategies that allow people to reshape their behavioural patterns. Psychological texts use this vocabulary to trace the pathways from environmental cues through habit formation to the behavioural outcomes that determine whether people act automatically or deliberately in response to the situations they encounter.

## Bias and Decision-Making（偏见与决策）

Cognitive bias（认知偏见）is a systematic tendency（系统性倾向）to think, judge, or act in ways that deviate from rational analysis（理性分析）. Biases arise from heuristics（启发式）— mental shortcuts that the brain uses to make decisions quickly and efficiently without analysing every detail. These shortcuts are usually adaptive: they allow fast decisions（快速决策）in situations where time is limited, information is incomplete, and thorough analysis is impractical. They can also produce systematic errors in judgement that are predictable, replicable, and resistant to correction（抵抗纠正）.

Confirmation bias（确认偏误）is the tendency to search for, interpret, favour, and recall information that confirms existing beliefs（现有信念）while ignoring, discounting（低估）, or forgetting information that contradicts them. When a person holds a strong opinion, they are more likely to notice evidence that supports it, interpret ambiguous evidence（模糊证据）as supporting their position, and remember supporting evidence more vividly than contradictory evidence. Confirmation bias makes beliefs self-reinforcing（自我强化的）— each piece of confirming evidence strengthens the belief, while disconfirming evidence is filtered out before it can challenge it. In scientific reasoning（科学推理）, confirmation bias leads researchers to favour evidence that supports their hypotheses and to discount evidence that contradicts them — which is why blind（盲法）and double-blind（双盲）experimental designs are necessary to prevent researcher expectations from distorting results.

Availability bias（可得性偏误）is the tendency to judge the probability（概率）of events based on how easily examples come to mind（想到例子的容易程度）rather than on actual statistical frequency（统计频率）. Events that are dramatic（戏剧性的）, recent（近期的）, emotionally vivid（情感生动的）, or widely reported in media are more easily recalled, so their frequency tends to be overestimated（高估）. Plane crashes（飞机失事）receive extensive media coverage and evoke strong emotional responses, leading people to overestimate their risk despite air travel being statistically far safer than driving. Common causes of death — heart disease（心脏病）, stroke（中风）, diabetes（糖尿病）— are underestimated（低估）because they lack dramatic media narratives（媒体叙事）. Availability bias distorts risk perception（风险感知）by substituting the question "How common is this?" with the easier question "How easily can I think of examples?"

Anchoring bias（锚定偏误）is the tendency to rely too heavily on the first piece of information encountered（首先接触到的信息）when making numerical estimates or decisions. The initial information serves as an anchor（锚点）, and subsequent judgements are made by adjusting away from it — but the adjustments are typically insufficient（不充分的）. When a product is shown at a high original price and then discounted, the original price anchors the perception of value（价值感知）, making the discounted price seem like a good deal even if it remains expensive in absolute terms. In salary negotiations（薪资谈判）, the first number proposed anchors the entire negotiation range. Anchoring effects are robust and persist even when people are explicitly warned about them and motivated to avoid them.

Overconfidence bias（过度自信偏误）is the tendency to overestimate one's own abilities, knowledge, or the accuracy of one's judgements. Most people rate themselves as above average（高于平均水平）in driving ability, intelligence, job performance, and ethical behaviour — which is statistically impossible since the majority cannot be above the median（中位数）. Overconfidence leads people to take excessive risks（过度冒险）, fail to prepare adequately（准备不足）, underestimate project completion times（低估项目完成时间）, and persist in failing courses of action（坚持失败的行动方向）. The Dunning-Kruger effect（邓宁-克鲁格效应）describes a specific form of overconfidence where people with low ability in a domain overestimate their competence because they lack the metacognitive skills（元认知技能）to recognise their own inadequacy — they do not know enough to know how much they do not know.

Framing effects（框架效应）occur when the same information presented in different ways（不同方式呈现相同信息）leads to different decisions. People are more likely to choose a medical treatment described as having a "90 percent survival rate"（90%存活率）than one described as having a "10 percent mortality rate"（10%死亡率）, even though the information is mathematically identical. This asymmetry reflects loss aversion（损失厌恶）— the tendency to prefer avoiding losses over acquiring equivalent gains（等量收益）. Losing $100 produces more psychological pain（心理痛苦）than gaining $100 produces pleasure, so people are more willing to take risks to avoid losses than to achieve gains. Framing effects have significant implications for medical decision-making（医疗决策）, financial choices（金融选择）, and public policy（公共政策）, where the way information is presented can systematically influence the decisions that people make.

Cognitive bias therefore represents the systematic patterns in human judgement that deviate from rational choice. The vocabulary of cognitive bias — confirmation bias, availability bias, anchoring bias, overconfidence bias, Dunning-Kruger effect, framing effect, loss aversion, heuristic — names the mental shortcuts that produce efficient but error-prone decisions and the conditions under which those shortcuts lead people away from rational analysis. Psychological texts use this vocabulary to trace the pathways from cognitive shortcuts through biased judgement to the decision outcomes that determine whether people make choices that serve their long-term interests or fall prey to predictable errors.

## Social Influence and Group Behaviour（社会影响与群体行为）

Social influence（社会影响）refers to the ways in which other people — their presence, actions, opinions, and expectations — affect an individual's thoughts, feelings, and behaviours. Human behaviour is profoundly social: people evolved in groups, depend on groups for survival and wellbeing, and are highly sensitive to social information（社会信息）. Social influence operates even when people are not consciously aware of its effects, shaping judgements, preferences, and actions through mechanisms that are often automatic and implicit（内隐的）.

Conformity（从众）is the tendency to align one's behaviour or opinions with those of a group. People conform for two distinct reasons. Normative social influence（规范性社会影响）occurs when people conform to gain social acceptance（社会接纳）and avoid rejection（排斥）— they want to fit in and avoid standing out. Informational social influence（信息性社会影响）occurs when people conform because they believe the group has more accurate information — they look to others for guidance in ambiguous or unfamiliar situations. In Solomon Asch's classic experiments（阿希经典实验）, participants judged which of three comparison lines matched a reference line in length. When confederates（实验同谋）deliberately gave wrong answers, many participants also gave wrong answers despite the correct answer being obvious. This conformity was driven primarily by normative pressure — participants knew the correct answer but conformed to avoid standing out or appearing deviant（偏离常态的）.

Obedience to authority（服从权威）is a powerful form of social influence where people comply with（遵从）instructions from someone perceived as a legitimate authority figure（合法权威人物）. In Stanley Milgram's experiments（米尔格拉姆实验）, participants were instructed to administer increasingly strong electric shocks（电击）to another person (a confederate) when that person answered questions incorrectly. Despite hearing cries of pain and pleas to stop, approximately sixty-five percent of participants continued to administer shocks up to the maximum level when instructed by the experimenter. The research demonstrated that situational factors（情境因素）— the presence of an authority figure, the gradual escalation（逐步升级）of demands, the physical distance from the victim, and the diffusion of responsibility（责任分散）— can influence behaviour more powerfully than most people expect or believe possible about themselves.

Group polarisation（群体极化）occurs when group discussion leads members to adopt more extreme positions（更极端的立场）than their initial individual positions. When a group of people who all moderately support a policy discuss it together, they are likely to emerge from the discussion strongly supporting it. This polarisation occurs through two mechanisms: persuasive arguments（说服性论证）— group members hear new arguments supporting their shared position that they had not previously considered, strengthening their conviction; and social comparison（社会比较）— members want to present themselves as more committed to the group's values than the average member, shifting the group norm（群体规范）toward the extreme. Group polarisation helps explain why political opinions（政治观点）often become more extreme when like-minded people（志同道合的人）discuss issues together in person or online, and why deliberative groups（审议群体）sometimes make more extreme decisions than individuals would make alone.

Social loafing（社会懈怠）is the tendency for individuals to exert less effort（付出更少努力）when working in a group than when working alone. When individual contributions cannot be identified and evaluated, people may reduce their effort because they feel less personally accountable（个人责任）for the outcome. Social loafing is reduced when the task is meaningful（有意义的）, when group members know each other（相互认识）, when individual contributions are identifiable（可识别的）and evaluable（可评估的）, and when the group is small enough that each member's contribution is noticeable. This phenomenon explains why group projects（小组项目）can sometimes be less productive than individual work and why organisations need to design accountability structures（问责结构）that maintain individual motivation within team settings.

The bystander effect（旁观者效应）describes the finding that people are less likely to help in an emergency（紧急情况）when other bystanders（旁观者）are present. The more bystanders there are, the less likely any individual is to intervene. This occurs through two psychological mechanisms: diffusion of responsibility（责任分散）— each bystander assumes that someone else will help, reducing the personal sense of obligation（个人义务感）; and pluralistic ignorance（多元无知）— each bystander looks to others to determine whether the situation is an emergency, and because everyone else appears calm (because they are also looking at others), everyone concludes that no emergency exists. The bystander effect can be overcome by making responsibility explicit（明确责任）— directly asking a specific person for help ("You in the red shirt, please call an ambulance") eliminates diffusion and dramatically increases the probability of receiving assistance.

Social influence therefore represents the mechanisms through which the presence and actions of others shape individual behaviour in groups. The vocabulary of social influence — conformity, normative social influence, informational social influence, obedience to authority, group polarisation, social loafing, bystander effect, diffusion of responsibility — names the processes through which groups influence individual behaviour and the conditions that determine whether social influence leads to cooperation, conformity, or inaction. Psychological texts use this vocabulary to trace the pathways from social context through psychological mechanisms to the behavioural outcomes that determine whether people act independently or in response to the presence and expectations of others.

## Experiments and Psychological Evidence（实验与心理学证据）

Psychology uses experiments（实验）to test hypotheses（假设）about human behaviour and mental processes. Psychological experiments follow the same scientific principles as experiments in other sciences: they manipulate independent variables（自变量）, control for confounding factors（混杂因素）, and collect data to test predictions. Psychology faces unique challenges because its subject matter — human thought, emotion, and behaviour — is complex, variable across individuals and contexts, influenced by many factors that are difficult to control or even identify, and sometimes altered by the very act of being studied.

Laboratory experiments（实验室实验）take place in controlled environments where conditions can be carefully managed and standardised. A researcher might bring participants into a lab, present different versions of a stimulus（刺激的不同版本）, and measure responses such as reaction time（反应时间）, accuracy（准确率）, physiological measures（生理指标）, or self-reported ratings（自我报告评分）. Lab experiments achieve high internal validity（内部效度）— confidence that observed effects were caused by the manipulated variable rather than by confounding factors — because the researcher controls the environment, the procedures, and the measurement. However, lab experiments may have limited external validity（外部效度）— the artificial setting and simplified tasks may not reflect how people think and behave in real-world situations where context, motivation, social pressure, and environmental complexity all influence behaviour.

Field experiments（现场实验）take place in real-world settings（真实环境）where participants may or may not know they are part of a study. Field experiments achieve higher external validity — results are more likely to generalise（推广）to natural behaviour — because they capture how people actually behave in their normal environments. The researcher has less control over extraneous variables（无关变量）, which can introduce noise（噪音）and confounding. A field experiment testing whether a new teaching method improves learning might be conducted in actual classrooms, but the researcher cannot control all the differences between classrooms, teachers, student populations, and school environments that might also affect outcomes. The trade-off between internal and external validity（内部效度与外部效度之间的权衡）means that laboratory and field experiments provide complementary evidence（互补证据）.

Correlational studies（相关研究）measure the relationship between two or more variables without manipulating any of them. A correlational study might find that students who sleep more hours tend to have higher grades（成绩）. This correlation（相关）does not establish causation（因果关系）. Three explanations are possible: more sleep causes better grades through improved memory consolidation（记忆巩固）and attention; higher academic performance (or the habits that produce it) causes better sleep through reduced stress; or a third factor — such as good time management（时间管理）, stable home environment, or lower anxiety — causes both better sleep and better grades. Correlational studies are valuable for identifying relationships that can be investigated further with experiments, for studying variables that cannot ethically or practically be manipulated（无法在伦理或实践上进行操纵的变量）, and for examining patterns in large populations. They cannot, by themselves, establish cause and effect.

The replication crisis（可重复性危机）in psychology has highlighted the importance of rigorous methodology（严格的方法论）and independent verification（独立验证）. Many well-known psychological findings have failed to replicate（未能重复）when later researchers repeated the studies with larger samples, more rigorous methods, and pre-registered analysis plans（预注册分析计划）. Factors contributing to the replication crisis include small sample sizes（小样本量）that produce unstable results, p-hacking（p值操纵）— analysing data in multiple ways until a statistically significant result is found, publication bias（发表偏倚）— journals' preference for publishing novel positive results over null results（零结果）or replications, and questionable research practices（可疑研究行为）such as selectively reporting measures or excluding data points that do not support the hypothesis. The field has responded by promoting larger samples, pre-registering studies（预注册研究）before data collection, sharing data and materials openly（公开共享数据和材料）, and conducting large-scale direct replications（大规模直接重复）before accepting findings as established.

Effect size（效应大小）measures the magnitude（幅度）of a finding — how large the difference between groups is, or how strong the relationship between variables is. A study might find a statistically significant（统计显著的）difference between two groups, but if the effect size is very small, the finding may have little practical importance（实际重要性）. Cohen's d（科恩d值）is a common effect size measure for group differences: a d of 0.2 is considered small, 0.5 medium, and 0.8 large. Reporting effect sizes alongside statistical significance allows readers to assess whether a finding is meaningful in practical terms, not merely detectable by statistical tests（统计检验）. Meta-analysis（荟萃分析）combines effect sizes from multiple studies to produce a more precise and reliable estimate（更精确可靠的估计）of the true effect, while also revealing heterogeneity（异质性）— variation in effect sizes across studies that may indicate moderating factors（调节因素）.

Psychological evidence therefore represents the mechanism through which psychologists design studies, evaluate evidence, and build reliable knowledge about the mental processes and social forces that shape human behaviour. The vocabulary of psychological evidence — internal validity, external validity, correlational study, replication crisis, p-hacking, publication bias, effect size, pre-registration — names the methodological standards that determine whether psychological findings are trustworthy and the practices that allow the field to distinguish reliable knowledge from artefacts of research design. Psychological texts use this vocabulary to trace the pathways from study design through evidence evaluation to the conclusions that determine whether psychological claims about human behaviour are supported by rigorous empirical evidence.
